newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. fights Time Warner in Murdoch dispute.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. fights Time Warner in Murdoch dispute.

text.p: New York City urged a federal appeals court Wednesday to overturn a temporary order won by Time Warner Inc. that is keeping Rupert Murdoch's Fox News off a city-run cable television channel.

In arguments before the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals, Elizabeth Freedman, a city lawyer, said that New York -- not cable operator Time Warner -- has the right to decide what is shown on its channels designated for "public, educational and governmental" (PEG) use.
"Time Warner never had First Amendment rights on the PEG channels," she told the three-member panel, which took the case under advisement.

Freedman argued the injunction should be thrown out because Time Warner had not met the requirement of showing it would be irreparably harmed if the Fox news programming was aired until the merits of the case are decided.
Time Warner provides cable service, including the city-run channels, to 1.1 million customers in New York.
Stuart Gold, a Time Warner lawyer, countered that federal law does give the cable company free speech rights to decide what is aired on the channels it provides.
"We are a fully protected First Amendment speaker. ... We are trying to stop their (New York City) misuse of editorial control," he said.

In November, U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that the city had violated Time Warner's First Amendment rights under the U.S. Constitution by trying to force Time Warner to carry the Fox programming and interfere with its editorial discretion.

She said New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, in an effort to help Murdoch, a political supporter, planned to air Fox News on a city-run cable channel to pressure Time Warner to carry it on a commercial station.
The order also prevents New York City from airing Bloomberg Information Television on a city-run channel.

Cote also said the city's efforts to air commercial 24-hour news programmes on the PEG channels was unprecedented and was never contemplated by Congress in the Federal Cable Act. She also found the city violated its own franchise agreement with Time Warner.

The dispute centres on the role of the city's five stations, known as "Crosswalks." Giuliani decided to place the new 24-hour Fox news programming without commercials on one of the Crosswalks channels after Time Warner rejected it.
He also planned to run Bloomberg's news programming.

Time Warner sued the city, alleging Giuliani was acting to please Murdoch, a prominent conservative whose News Corp. Ltd. owns the New York Post and WNYW-TV,a broadcast channel. It said in its lawsuit that the city was acting as Murdoch's "latest political puppet."
